oneSentence: A citation in an AI answer points you to a source passage or document intended to support a specific claim.
plainExplanation:
When an AI system gives an answer with citations, it presents sources as support for parts of that answer. The source might be a web page, a report, a policy document or a passage from a knowledge base. The useful part is not the label alone, but the link between the claim and the supporting text.

A common process starts with a question. The system searches a set of documents and retrieves passages that seem relevant. “Retrieve” here means find and bring back likely source text. The model then drafts an answer from the passages, and the system attaches references intended to support particular claims.

What goes in is your question and a collection of documents. What happens is search, selection and answer drafting. What comes out is an answer plus citations, often as footnotes, numbered references or quoted snippets.

A citation is not the same as proof. It can point to a weak source, the wrong passage or a passage that only partly supports the answer. It is also not the same as grounding. Grounding ties an answer to retrieved source passages; a citation is the visible pointer that helps a person check that connection.

For a reader, the main value is verification. You can open the cited source, see the original wording, check the date and judge whether the answer represented it fairly.

everydayAnalogy.title: Matching a photographed form to the right template
everydayAnalogy.story: A clinic worker in Dakar receives a phone photo of a paper form. The image is unclear, so she compares it with a folder of known form templates and finds the one with the same layout and field labels. When she tells her colleague which form it is, she also clips the matching template page to her note so the colleague can check it directly. The clipped page does not guarantee that every handwritten entry was read correctly, but it gives everyone a concrete place to verify the match.

mapping.analogyElement: the phone photo of the form

mapping.aiElement: the document collection or knowledge base
the retrieved source passage or document

mapping.analogyElement: clipping the template page to the note
mapping.aiElement: adding a citation to the answer

everydayAnalogy.limitation: In the story, a person deliberately compares visible layouts. In AI systems, matching is often done mathematically from text or embeddings, which are numerical representations of meaning-like patterns. Also, a cited passage in an AI answer may support only one sentence or part of a sentence, not the whole answer. The analogy also makes the match seem clearer than it often is: real retrieval can return several partly relevant passages, and the model may cite one imperfectly.

visual.title: How citations get attached to an AI answer
visual.learningObjective: After viewing this, a reader should be able to say that citations come from retrieved source passages and are there to help people verify claims.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow with five boxes connected by arrows. Read from the user’s question to document search, then retrieved passages, then drafted answer, then answer with citation markers linked back to the passages. Small callout text under the final box says: “Helpful for checking, not automatic proof.”

visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram shows a five-step process. First, a user asks a question. Second, the system searches a collection of documents. Third, it retrieves a small number of relevant passages. Fourth, the model drafts an answer using those passages. Fifth, the answer displays citation markers, such as small numbers, that point back to the specific passages. The main message is that citations are pointers to supporting text, so a person can verify claims, but the presence of a citation alone does not guarantee the answer is correct.

workedExample.scenario: An OHCHR desk officer in Lima is finalising a background note for a Human Rights Council side event and asks an approved assistant what the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence says about transparency.
workedExample.input: The question and an indexed collection containing 41 C/Resolution 15 and other approved public documents.
process: The retrieval step ranks passages that mention transparency and explainability, including passages from 41 C/Resolution 15.
The model drafts a short summary using the retrieved context and places a source link after each substantive claim.
The desk officer opens the cited passages and checks whether each one supports the precise wording, rather than merely mentioning the same topic.
One broad claim is narrowed because its citation supports a more qualified formulation. The revised background note then goes into clearance.
workedExample.result: The citations make the answer auditable and help the desk officer correct an overstatement before the background note is circulated.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A statistician in a Lima data unit is checking a statement for delivery before the front office sends it for clearance at close of business. An approved assistant links each figure and trend in the draft to the relevant passage or table in the latest published monitoring report.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: The citations give the statistician a direct route from each claim to its supporting text or table. This makes it easier to catch a citation that points to the right report but the wrong passage, or to a passage that does not support the wording used.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: A citation is not proof that the claim is correct. The statistician must open the cited passage, confirm that the reporting period, definition and denominator match, and check that the source is current. Unpublished microdata or records containing personal information must not be entered into a tool that is not approved for them.

whyItMatters: For non-specialists, citations change an AI answer from something you can only read into something you can inspect. That matters when a sentence may affect a briefing, a public statement, a procurement note or a policy discussion. A citation helps you ask practical questions: Where did this come from? Is the source authoritative? Is it current? Does the source really support this exact claim? Without that check, an answer can sound confident while resting on weak or mismatched material. With citations, verification becomes faster, but it still depends on human judgement.

When a desk officer opens a cited passage and finds only a keyword match
In a procurement meeting reviewing citation and source-linking requirements

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If an AI answer has citations, the answer is reliable.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Citations help, but reliability depends on what was cited and how accurately the answer used it. A system can attach an outdated source, cite a passage that only partly supports the claim, or misread the passage. You still need to inspect the source.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A citation always points to the exact sentence that proves the claim.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Some systems cite a whole document, a page or a chunk of text rather than the precise line. That can still be useful, but it means the reader may need to look around the cited passage and judge whether the support is strong enough.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Citation and grounding mean the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.correction: They are related, but not identical. Grounding is the broader practice of tying an answer to external evidence or data. A citation is the visible reference shown to the user. A system can attempt grounding without showing clear citations, and a citation can be shown even if the support is weak.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: A citation is the “show me where that came from” part of an AI answer.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: In retrieval-augmented systems, citations are usually produced after a retrieval step selects relevant documents or chunks from an indexed collection. The model then generates a response conditioned on that retrieved context, and the system links claims to source items, passages or spans. Depending on the system design, source references may be selected before generation, emitted during generation or aligned with claims later. Citation quality depends on retrieval quality, chunking, ranking, source metadata and how accurately the system maps answer claims back to evidence. This is why a citation is best treated as traceability support, not as a guarantee of factual correctness.

keyTakeaway: A good citation lets you trace an AI claim back to source text, but you still need to check whether the source actually supports that specific claim.

quickCheck.question: What is the main purpose of a citation in an AI answer?
options: To make the answer sound more academic
To point the reader to the source used so the claim can be checked
To guarantee that the answer is correct
To replace the need to read the original document
quickCheck.explanation: The core job of a citation is traceability. It helps a reader inspect the original source and judge whether the answer used it correctly. It does not by itself guarantee accuracy, and it does not remove the need for human review.

issues.problem: The definition treats a citation as evidence that the cited source was actually used. A citation only presents a source as support. It may have been attached later, mismatched or invented.
issues.fix: A citation in an AI answer points you to a source passage or document intended to support a specific claim.

issues.problem: The phrases “shows where parts of that answer came from” and “passages it used” confuse a visible citation with verified provenance. The explanation also calls grounding the broader idea of connection to any external material, which contradicts the supplied definition tying grounding to specific retrieved passages.
issues.fix: Replace the field with the corrected plain explanation below.

issues.problem: This defines grounding as connection to any external evidence or data. That contradicts the separate entry, which defines grounding as tying an answer to specific retrieved source passages.
issues.fix: They are related, but not identical. Grounding ties an answer to retrieved source passages so it is based on provided material. A citation is the visible reference shown to the user. A system can be grounded without showing clear citations, and a citation can appear even when the source does not support the claim.

issues.problem: It says the interface attaches references, then says citations may be linked during generation. The interface is not universally responsible for citation attachment. Some models emit citation markers, while other system components align claims and sources later.
